claim: The wāw of wa-l-ʿaṣr is the particle of oath (wāw al-qasam), not a conjunction joining two things, which is why al-ʿaṣr is in the genitive.
The thing sworn to (the answer of the oath) is not stated in 103:1 but in 103:2, inna l-insāna la-fī khusr; the first verse is a threshold whose ruling is withheld until the next verse.

What is sworn by is placed right beside the ruling it introduces, so that understanding what al-ʿaṣr is shows what kind of loss (khusr) is meant: the oath-object and the statement of loss are linked in meaning.
Wa-l-fajr (89:1), wa-l-ḍuḥā (93:1), wa-l-layli idhā yaghshā (92:1) and wa-l-ṣubḥi idhā asfar (74:34) are cited as the Qurʾān's other oaths by times of day, the group to which wa-l-ʿaṣr belongs.

Unlike most of these time-oaths, where the time comes with a motion or qualifier (idhā yaghshā, idhā asfar), al-ʿaṣr stands alone with no qualification, and this bareness leaves the word's range of meaning open.

Lexically al-ʿaṣr names both time at large and a part of the day: al-ʿaṣr = al-dahr (a long time, an age) and al-ʿaṣr = al-ʿashiyy (late afternoon), and the afternoon prayer, ṣalāt al-ʿaṣr, takes its name from that hour.

The definite article points to a known time, but 103:1 does not say whether the afternoon of the day, the age in which man lives, or time itself is meant; the paragraph does not choose one referent and leaves all three to be heard together.

Turkish has split the word: 'asır' now means century ('asri' contemporary) while the end of the day is 'ikindi', so the Turkish word loses the afternoon sense and the root's senses of pressing, refuge and whirlwind.
The Qurʾānic word holds the hour and the age together, so that the end of a day and the end of a lifetime bear the same name.
The Arabs used the dual al-ʿaṣrān for the two ends of the day: night and day (al-layl wa-l-nahār), or early morning and late afternoon (al-ghadāh wa-l-ʿashiyy).
The phrase bi-l-ghadāti wa-l-ʿashiyy in 6:52 (the believers calling on their Lord morning and evening) is cited as the Qurʾān's own naming of the pair of day-ends that al-ʿaṣrān denotes.
The phrase ṭarafayi l-nahār in 11:114, giving the times of prayer, is cited as another Qurʾānic naming of the day's two ends, the pair called al-ʿaṣrān.
That ʿaṣr names the two ends of the day shows the word grasps time at its edge, where a period is entered and left; the afternoon sense in 103:1 is one such edge, the closing end of the day.
The root carries lateness: jāʾanī fulānun ʿaṣran means someone came late, slowly.
ʿAṣr also names a brief stretch, even a moment: nāma wa-mā nāma li-ʿaṣr (he lay down but did not sleep a moment) and al-ʿaṣār = al-ḥīn (a while); so ʿaṣr is both a long age and an instant.
ʿAṣr names stages of a human life: of a girl, balaghat ʿaṣra shabābihā wa-idrākihā (she reached the age of youth and maturity), and a person's lifetime and old age are also called by this name.

The late-afternoon sense is read as time running short: the hour when least of the day remains and time narrows for what is undone, so that al-ʿaṣr is not only an hour but the lateness felt within it.

Lam yalbathū illā ʿashiyyatan aw ḍuḥāhā (79:46), answering the question about the Hour (79:42), is cited as the Qurʾān's instance of a whole lifetime shrinking, seen from the end, into one part of a day; the paragraph uses ʿashiyya, the afternoon by which ʿaṣr is glossed, to show how the long age and the afternoon held in al-ʿaṣr turn into each other from the end.
The plea of the people of Hell in 35:37, rabbanā akhrijnā naʿmal ṣāliḥan, is cited as the Qurʾān's open instance of the work left too late, the lateness the paragraph hears in ʿaṣr.

The reply in 35:37, a-wa-lam nuʿammirkum mā yatadhakkaru fīhi man tadhakkar, is read as naming life as an allotted span given for reflection; the loss of 103:2 and the faith and righteous deeds of 103:3 are placed within this given span, i.e. al-ʿaṣr is heard as the lifetime granted.
The root's most concrete sense is pressing: ḍaghṭu shayʾin ḥattā yataḥallab, pressing a thing until its liquid flows out.
The images drawn from the pressing sense do not replace the sense of 'time' in 103:1 but are heard alongside it; the paragraph keeps time as the verse's meaning.

The vocabulary of pressing grapes: al-miʿṣār is a bag like a feed-bag in which grapes are pressed, al-maʿṣara the place of pressing, al-ʿuṣāra what flows from pressing, and ʿaṣīr anything whose juice has been pressed; the dregs remain in the bag.
Pressing divides a thing in two: the essence that flows away and the dry mass left behind.

The Arabs made al-ʿuṣāra and al-muʿtaṣar a figure for good and giving: of a generous man, yaʿṣiru fīnā ka-lladhī taʿṣir (he gives to us as you give), and al-ʿuṣāra also means al-ghalla, the yield of land.
Pressing is carried to the sky: al-muʿṣirāt are clouds pressed with rain, saḥāba muʿṣir a cloud that yields rain as if milked, and ʿuṣira l-qawm means the people were rained upon.

Al-muʿṣirāt in 78:14 (wa-anzalnā mina l-muʿṣirāti māʾan thajjājā) is taken as the rain clouds 'pressed' with rain, the Qurʾān naming these clouds with the root's word; other identifications of al-muʿṣirāt are not considered.
78:14-16, addressed to those disputing the news of the Resurrection, are read as a chain of blessing set off by the pressing of clouds: pressed cloud, then grain, plants and dense gardens.
The other end of pressing is dryness: al-maʿṣūr is the tongue dried out by thirst, a pressed tongue with no water left in it.
The same verb names a movement of rescue: al-iʿtiṣār is when one chokes on food and sips water little by little to get it down.
The poet's verse law bi-ghayri l-māʾi ḥalqī shariqun kuntu ka-l-ghaṣṣāni bi-l-māʾi ʿtiṣārī is read as turning that image round: what chokes him is water itself, so no rescuing sip remains.

Heard beside the time of 103:1, these images show time as pressure: the days pass over a person and draw something out of him, either an essence that flows as gift, like rain from a cloud, or a dry mass like a thirst-dried tongue.
The loss (khusr) of 103:2 is read as the dry remainder of what has been pressed.
Ṣabr, the last word of 103:3, is also the name of a bitter juice pressed from a tree (aloe), which carries the pressing image to the end of the sura.

Ḥattā ḥīn in 12:35 is read as measuring Joseph's imprisonment by a span of time, and linked to ʿaṣr meaning a stretch of time and also detention (al-ḥabs); the paragraph says this is a connection, not shared wording, since the Qurʾān uses another word (sijn) for the prison.
In aʿṣiru khamran (12:36) what the youth presses is grapes, but the sentence names it by the drink that will come of it: pressing is named by its product.

Joseph's interpretation in 12:41 (fa-yasqī rabbahu khamran) is read as rescue for this youth, and 12:42 calls him the one who would be saved (nājin): the one who presses in his dream is the one who leaves the prison.
The lexical sense al-ʿaṣr = al-manjāh (place of rescue, escape) is heard echoing in this scene.
In 12:42 it is the freed youth who forgets to mention Joseph to his master, and this forgetting prolongs Joseph's stay in prison by biḍʿa sinīn (some years).
Wa-ddakara baʿda umma in 12:45 is read as 'remembered after a long while' (umma as a span of time).

Joseph's interpretation of the king's dream of seven green and seven dry ears (12:43) is read as a time plan: seven years of sowing with the harvest left in its ears (fa-dharūhu fī sunbulihi, 12:47), then seven hard years that eat what was stored except a little kept back (tuḥṣinūn, 12:48).

When the sheaths of the ears appear, the Arabs said qad aʿṣara l-zarʿ, derived from al-ʿaṣr meaning al-ḥirz (protection) because the grain is guarded in its sheath; the paragraph links this to Joseph's plan of keeping grain in its ear, while noting the Qurʾān's word there is sunbul, not ʿaṣr.
Yaʿṣirūn in 12:49 is read as 'they press' (the year of relief in which pressing resumes) and is also reported as understood to mean 'they gain yield from their lands' (yastaghillūna bi-araḍīhim).

In the Joseph story the root's seemingly distant senses fall into one calendar: time spent in prison, pressing in the dream of the one to be rescued, forgotten and lengthening years, grain kept in its sheath, and the year of plenty when pressing begins again.
Pressing in this story marks the end of scarcity: the grapes to be pressed are the share of those who waited patiently through the hard years and stored.
Seen this way, the time sworn by in 103:1 is not only a span that consumes but one in which what is stored is protected and finally pressed out and flows.
Al-ʿaṣr also means holding back: al-ʿaṣr = al-ḥabs, and mā ʿaṣaraka means 'what held you back, prevented you'.
One who holds on and does not give is called ʿāṣir (= mumsik, tight-fisted).

The verb also names withholding and taking back property: yaʿtaṣiru l-wālidu ʿalā waladihi fī mālihi (the father withholds his child's property from him) and aʿṭaytu fulānan ʿaṭiyyatan fa-ʿtaṣartuhā (I gave a gift and then took it back).

The same verb can name both open-handedness (the generous man who yaʿṣiru) and tight-fistedness, because both are gripping something in the hand; the difference is whether anything flows out of the grip.
Al-muʿṣir is a girl at the time of her first menstruation, so called because she is kept in the house and given a shelter (ʿaṣr); the grain kept in its sheath is within the same kind of shelter.
Holding is not always blameworthy: here it means protecting one who stands at a threshold.

The story of the owners of the garden (68:17-27), who swore to harvest at dawn and meant to keep every poor person out (68:24), is cited as the Qurʾān's instance of what withholding produce brings: the withheld harvest did not stay in the withholders' hands (68:19-20, 68:26-27).
Wa-lā yastathnūn (68:18) is read as 'they made no exception' in their oath.
Fa-aṣbaḥat ka-l-ṣarīm (68:20) is read as the garden turning out at morning cut down and black.
The garden owners swore an oath without exception, whereas the sura's oath is completed by the general ruling of 103:2 followed by the exception (illā) of 103:3.

The root denotes clinging: taʿalluq bi-shayʾ wa-imtisāk bihi (hanging on to a thing and holding it tight), and the place clung to is called al-ʿaṣr = al-maljaʾ (refuge); iʿtaṣartu bi-fulān / taʿaṣṣartu means I took refuge with someone, and iʿtaṣara bi-l-makān he took refuge in a place.
The idiom ʿuṣrat al-manjūd ties this refuge to the hard-pressed: the refuge of one in distress.
The bond between two people is named by the word through its absence: mā baynahumā ʿaṣrun wa-lā yaṣr, there is neither affection nor kinship between them.
Al-ʿunṣur (root, lineage) is said to come from al-ʿaṣr in the sense of refuge, with an added nūn: one's lineage is where one turns for refuge.
Al-maʿāṣir, coats of mail, are said to derive from al-ʿaṣr because one is protected by them.

That one word names both squeezing and refuge is only an apparent contradiction: both are a grip. Pressing wraps a thing from outside, the one taking refuge grips something tightly, armour wraps and protects the body; the hard-pressed run to refuge, as the idiom ʿuṣrat al-manjūd says.
Heard beside the time of 103:1, this image makes the time sworn by both a span that presses man and a place of refuge.

The youths' taking refuge in the cave (fa-ʾwū ilā l-kahf, 18:16; idh awā l-fityatu ilā l-kahf, 18:10) and their sleep (fa-ḍarabnā ʿalā ādhānihim, 18:11) are cited as the Qurʾān's instance of a refuge that closes time off.

The sleepers' estimate labithnā yawman aw baʿḍa yawm (18:19) is set against wa-labithū fī kahfihim thalātha miʾatin sinīna wa-zdādū tisʿā (18:25), which the paragraph takes as the true length of their stay.
The Cave story shows three faces of ʿaṣr together, refuge, a long age, and the span the sleeper takes for a moment, though the word itself does not occur there.
The believers excepted in 103:3 lean on this refuge image: deliverance from loss is heard as taking refuge.

Al-iʿṣār is a wind that blows, raises dust and lifts it to the sky like a column, and also the dust that rises in a spiral (plural aʿāṣīr): a wind that gathers what is on the ground by turning it and draws it up as an upright column.
The same branch describes rising scent: of a perfumed woman passing, li-dhaylihā ʿaṣar (scent rises behind her train), and al-ʿuṣra is the wafting and stirring of perfume.
What links whirlwind and scent is a single motion: what swells and rises behind a moving thing is either dust or fragrance.
Iʿṣārun fīhi nārun fa-ḥtaraqat in 2:266 is cited as the Qurʾān's use of the iʿṣār whirlwind, set in a parable of a garden whose owner has reached old age with weak children.

The 2:266 parable is read in the series of parables on spending in God's way: after 2:264 (spending for show, like soil on a smooth rock washed bare by a downpour) and 2:265 (spending for God's pleasure, a hillside garden yielding double), and closing with kadhālika yubayyinu llāhu lakumu l-āyāti laʿallakum tatafakkarūn.

In the 2:266 garden several senses of the root stand together though only iʿṣār occurs as a word: grapes (aʿnāb, fruit to be pressed), rivers and all produce (yield), old age (al-kibar) as the afternoon of a life, and the fiery whirlwind that destroys it all.
The produce awaited a lifetime is lost just when its owner has no strength left to plant again; this is read as the most concrete picture of the loss (khusr) of 103:2.
Heard beside al-ʿaṣr, the whirlwind is the face of time that can scatter in a moment what time has accumulated.
The rising of scent stands at the other end of the same motion: behind one who passes, a fragrant trace rather than dust may remain.
